doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: What 'second line' means
summary: Stewart defines second line, names his First Line Band, and describes the groove.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Just so I have another sort of definition, second line, can you tell a student who might be watching this, what does he mean by that?

Second line? The literal translation is literally the second line, and the second line of musicians in most bands is the drum line, the drum line, the tuba, bass drum, snare drums, cymbals. It’s the second line. And on stage it’s the second line. When a sound guy talks about, “Yeah I’ll bring in the second line today,” he’s bringing in the amplifiers, the drum kit, and so forth and so on, which is the reason I name one of my bands the First Line Band, it’s just a play off of, I’m putting myself in the first line, thank you very much. So we call it Bob Stewart’s First Line Band. But it’s physically the second line. And then the techniques that are used by that second line in New Orleans gives the name of the music they play Second Line Music. It transcends the literal term to a kind of a more active term, Second Line Music.

It’s a way of playing the groove, playing second line with that accent on four and it’s coming off the tango. In the Latin music it’s the clave but they don’t end up playing the clave. I recently have taken a turn about the clave, I don’t want to digress or anything, but the music of Benin in Africa.
